summary:
TWINBOUND is a browser-based space mission design game where players compete through piloting, engineering, and scientific discovery. Choose the Moon, Mars, Pluto, or an idealized Proxima Centauri journey; design a spacecraft, select a science objective, plan a launch, and fly in 2D/3D.

NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides power date-dependent 11-body gravity and navigation. NASA Mission Design Lab and science-mission guidance inform engineering trade-offs and measurable goals; CubeSat 101 contributes transferable systems-engineering lessons. NASA Mission Viz's orbital tutorial informs a separate trajectory analysis that explains orbital elements in flight reports—not the live multi-body physics or score.

Competition connects engineering decisions to outcomes: Final Score = Arcade Score + NASA Mission Bonus. Within the bonus, mission requirements count 15%, measured engineering performance 20%, valid science return 60%, and qualified cost efficiency 5%. These are game-defined weights, not NASA standards. Detailed reports and a browser-local leaderboard encourage experimentation and replay.
details:
TWINBOUND — Space Mission Design Game

Play TWINBOUND Online: https://a0752074.github.io/TWINBOUND/

Source Code & Technical Documentation: https://github.com/a0752074/TWINBOUND

TWINBOUND is a free, browser-based space mission design game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Anyone can play directly through the website without installation, registration, or special hardware.

1. Our Vision

What if designing a space mission could become a game where scientific knowledge, engineering decisions, and piloting skills determine who wins?

TWINBOUND transforms NASA data and space mission-development concepts into an interactive adventure.

Rather than simply simulating spacecraft motion, we wanted players to experience how different engineering choices affect mission performance.

A successful mission requires more than reaching a destination. Players must balance scientific objectives, propulsion, spacecraft mass, available energy, communication capabilities, mission lifetime, and cost.

Our central idea is to make these decisions measurable and competitive, encouraging players to discover better mission designs through experimentation.

2. How the Game Works

Players choose one of four destinations:

  • Moon — Beginner: Introduction to orbital navigation and spacecraft design.
  • Mars — Intermediate: More demanding trajectory planning and resource management.
  • Pluto — Hard: Long-distance exploration with challenging mission constraints.
  • Proxima Centauri — Expert: An idealized interstellar journey exploring special relativity and time dilation.

Before launch, players configure propulsion, structure, power systems, scientific instruments, communications equipment, launch services, and mission budgets.

They then select a launch date and adjust departure direction and velocity while examining a predicted trajectory.

After launch, players enter an interactive 2D/3D flight experience, making fuel-consuming course corrections, avoiding obstacles, collecting resources, and maintaining trajectory stability.

Scientific operations introduce additional challenges involving instrument compatibility, battery energy, data storage, communication delays, and valid scientific observations.

At the end of each flight, a mission report explains the engineering performance, scientific results, and final score.

3. NASA Data and Resource Integration

NASA resources influence TWINBOUND in different ways: some provide actual scientific data, while others inform mission planning, engineering methods, and educational gameplay.

NASA/JPL Horizons — Scientific Data and Orbital Physics

NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides provide date-dependent positions and velocities for eleven moving Solar System gravity sources.

These data support the game's multi-body gravitational calculations, trajectory planning, spacecraft navigation, and communication-distance calculations.

The simulation combines Newtonian gravity with adaptive numerical integration, including a Dormand–Prince solver and Lambert-transfer-based planning.

Changing the launch date changes the celestial configuration and can affect the predicted trajectory.

Unlike a fixed animation, the spacecraft's simulated state responds to gravitational dynamics and player-controlled propulsion.

NASA Goddard Mission Design Lab — Engineering Trade-offs

NASA's Mission Design Lab provides an important methodological reference for evaluating spacecraft design alternatives.

Its multidisciplinary approach inspires our consideration of propulsion, spacecraft mass, power, communications, data capacity, and mission cost.

These principles are translated into interactive player choices.

For example, a high-performance propulsion system may improve maneuvering capabilities but increase cost and mass. More capable communications equipment may improve scientific data delivery while consuming additional power.

These decisions affect measurable engineering outcomes and contribute to the mission's evaluation.

NASA Design and Develop Science Missions — Mission Requirements

NASA's science mission-development resources inform how scientific objectives can be translated into measurable requirements.

Players must choose appropriate instruments, satisfy engineering constraints, and generate valid scientific observations.

For Solar System missions, scientific return is based on compatible observations and data successfully received on Earth.

The idealized Proxima Centauri mission uses an onboard scientific archive because of extreme communication delays.

This connects mission planning to actual scientific results rather than rewarding players solely for reaching their destination.

NASA CubeSat 101 — Transferable Systems-Engineering Lessons

NASA CubeSat 101 is a guide for developing small satellites, not a general design standard for every spacecraft.

TWINBOUND does not represent its fictional spacecraft as CubeSats or claim compliance with CubeSat hardware specifications.

Instead, we adapt transferable systems-engineering concepts from the guide, including early mission planning, requirements verification, launch constraints, spacecraft resources, and mission operations.

These concepts support a broader educational approach to spacecraft design.

In the playable game, four existing mission-design checks evaluate:

  • Scientific instrument compatibility
  • Wet mass relative to launch-service capacity
  • Budget compliance
  • Mission lifetime

These game-defined requirements influence mission evaluation. A separate CubeSat-inspired technical review provides additional research evidence but does not independently award gameplay points.

The same general engineering principles can be explored across different mission scenarios without treating all spacecraft as CubeSats.

4. NASA-Inspired Scoring and Player Competition

The central innovation of TWINBOUND is translating NASA-inspired mission requirements and engineering trade-offs into a competitive scoring system.

Players are not rewarded only for surviving, collecting resources, or reaching their destination.

They are also evaluated on how effectively they design, operate, and complete their scientific missions.

The final ranking score is:

Final Score = Arcade Score + NASA Mission Bonus

The Arcade Score retains the original gameplay rewards for navigation, survival, resource collection, near misses, and mission progress.

The NASA Mission Bonus uses four weighted dimensions:

15% — Mission Requirements

Evaluates scientific instrument compatibility, launch mass, budget, and mission lifetime. The reward is scaled by actual flight progress.

20% — Engineering Performance

Evaluates measured battery reserves, remaining fuel, and scientific data integrity. These outcomes are also scaled by actual flight progress.

60% — Scientific Return

Measures valid scientific data relative to the selected objective. Only compatible scientific results count; for Solar System missions, the data must actually reach Earth.

5% — Cost Efficiency

Rewards qualified cost-efficient spacecraft designs, but only when the complete mission satisfies all success requirements.

These weights apply within the Mission Bonus. They are educational game-balancing choices inspired by NASA mission-design principles, not official NASA scoring standards.

Each destination also has its own bonus cap, reflecting different mission difficulties.

Why This Makes Competition Meaningful

A cheaper spacecraft may receive a stronger arcade multiplier, but its limited capabilities can make scientific success more difficult.

A more expensive spacecraft may provide better propulsion, power, or communication capabilities, yet its higher cost does not automatically guarantee a higher score.

Likewise, reaching a destination does not guarantee full mission success if the spacecraft fails to satisfy its requirements or return sufficient scientific data.

Players must consider both piloting performance and mission design.

The highest score requires a balance of spacecraft engineering, efficient resource management, successful scientific observations, and skillful flight.

This creates a direct educational connection between NASA-inspired mission planning and competitive gameplay.

5. Leaderboard and Replayability

TWINBOUND includes a browser-local leaderboard supporting multiple Player IDs on the same browser.

Each destination maintains its own rankings, allowing players to compete within the same mission difficulty.

Scores include both Arcade achievements and the NASA Mission Bonus.

Every completed or failed flight is automatically recorded, and players can inspect its mission report, spacecraft configuration, scientific results, and score breakdown.

By comparing previous attempts, players can identify why one spacecraft design performed better than another.

They can experiment with different budgets, propulsion systems, scientific instruments, launch dates, and flight strategies.

The leaderboard requires no account or external database. Records are stored locally in the browser rather than shared globally.

Our goal is to encourage players to improve their understanding of space mission design as they compete for better results.

6. Creativity and Educational Value

TWINBOUND combines three experiences:

Scientific Simulation

Real NASA/JPL ephemeris data, orbital mechanics, gravitational dynamics, numerical integration, and an educational relativistic interstellar model.

Space Mission Engineering

Spacecraft configuration, engineering requirements, launch constraints, scientific objectives, energy management, communications, and mission costs.

Interactive Gameplay

Real-time spacecraft controls, obstacles, resource collection, mission progress, scientific achievements, and competitive scoring.

By connecting these elements, TWINBOUND transforms abstract scientific concepts into decisions that players can observe and evaluate.

The distinction between real NASA data, NASA-inspired engineering methods, and fictional gameplay assumptions is maintained throughout the project.

7. Technologies and Development

TWINBOUND is developed primarily using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Canvas, SVG, Web Audio, and browser Web Workers.

Python and JavaScript development tools support scientific data preparation, testing, and validation.

The browser-based application uses bundled NASA/JPL Horizons data and can be accessed directly through GitHub Pages.

OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex were extensively used to assist with programming, debugging, testing, English localization, and technical documentation.

The participant directed the original game concept, gameplay mechanics, scientific objectives, feature decisions, and iterative development.

The project distinguishes NASA-derived scientific information from educational assumptions, including fictional equipment prices, hardware specifications, and gameplay scoring weights.

Its public GitHub repository includes the source code, NASA resource references, physics documentation, scoring implementation, and technical evidence.

8. Intended Impact

TWINBOUND aims to make space mission design accessible, enjoyable, and competitive.

We want students, educators, and space enthusiasts to discover how science, engineering, and resource constraints shape the success of space missions.

By turning NASA-inspired mission requirements into measurable gameplay outcomes, players can learn through experimentation rather than memorization.

They can explore different spacecraft designs, understand engineering trade-offs, improve their scientific results, and challenge their friends to achieve higher scores.

Explore space. Design smarter missions. Challenge your friends. Learn through every flight.
